message:
fix(directory): the client's address is the observation, or there is none

When a request carried no address observation the server used the address
of the HTTP socket it arrived on, and a port the client claimed for itself
in the body. That address is the client's only when nothing sits in
between. Behind a proxy, a load balancer or a TLS terminator it is the
middle box's, so every host that heartbeats without an observation is
published at one address: the punch packets go to the middle box, which is
not listening, and two unrelated accounts become indistinguishable exactly
where relay eligibility is decided.

The fallback is gone rather than corrected. The observation is the only
thing that knows the port NAT actually mapped, so a request without one has
nothing to publish, and saying so is the whole answer.

409, not 401. Nothing is wrong with the caller's credentials, and a 401
would send a host to re-register and a viewer to sign in again -- neither of
which produces an observation. The reason is named: observation_required
when there is no record, observation_expired when there is one and it is too
old. Those call for different things from the client, and they used to be
the same absent entry because the sweep deleted expired records on sight;
it now keeps them past expiry long enough to answer the question.

The refusal happens before anything is written. Not lastSeen, which would
keep a host listed as online while publishing an address nobody can reach,
and not the pending punch, which the heartbeat consumes on read -- a
refused heartbeat that ate a punch would strand a viewer that did
everything right.

The comment above the old function said it honoured a trusted proxy header
when configured. Nothing there read a header, configured or not.

On the client, one retry and no more. The host sends a fresh observation
from the socket it streams on and heartbeats once more; if that is refused
too it says so and waits for the ordinary 25-second cycle. The viewer does
the same around /api/connect. Neither loops, neither signs out, and neither
touches a stream in progress -- the socket is only used to send a probe on.

The regression runs its own server behind its own TCP proxy, so every
request arrives from an address that is not the client's: signup, login,
register, heartbeat, hosts, connect and healthz all still work, the refusals
are 409 with the right name, the published port is the observed one and not
one the proxy connected on, and a refused connect leaves no punch behind.

The restart test asked for a heartbeat without an observation. It now
asserts both halves -- the restored token is recognised (409, not 401) and
then works with an observation -- because asserting only the 200 would have
let the new 409 read as "the token did not survive", which is the opposite
of true.
